source: It was nearly six o’clock, but only grey imperfect misty dawn, when we drew nigh the wharf.
“There are some sailors running ahead there, if I see right,” said I to Queequeg, “it can’t be shadows; she’s off by sunrise, I guess; come on!”

“Avast!” cried a voice, whose owner at the same time coming close behind us, laid a hand upon both our shoulders, and then insinuating himself between us, stood stooping forward a little, in the uncertain twilight, strangely peering from Queequeg to me. It was Elijah.
“Going aboard?”
“Hands off, will you,” said I.
“Lookee here,” said Queequeg, shaking himself, “go ’way!”
“Ain’t going aboard, then?”
“Yes, we are,” said I, “but what business is that of yours? Do you know, Mr. Elijah, that I consider you a little impertinent?”
“No, no, no; I wasn’t aware of that,” said Elijah, slowly and wonderingly looking from me to Queequeg, with the most unaccountable glances.
“Elijah,” said I, “you will oblige my friend and me by withdrawing. We are going to the Indian and Pacific Oceans, and would prefer not to be detained.”
“Ye be, be ye? Coming back afore breakfast?”
“He’s cracked, Queequeg,” said I, “come on.”
“Holloa!” cried stationary Elijah, hailing us when we had removed a few paces.
“Never mind him,” said I, “Queequeg, come on.”
But he stole up to us again, and suddenly clapping his hand on my shoulder, said—“Did ye see anything looking like men going towards that ship a while ago?”
Struck by this plain matter-of-fact question, I answered, saying, “Yes, I thought I did see four or five men; but it was too dim to be sure.”
“Very dim, very dim,” said Elijah. “Morning to ye.”
Once more we quitted him; but once more he came softly after us; and touching my shoulder again, said, “See if you can find ’em now, will ye?
“Find who?”

“Morning to ye! morning to ye!” he rejoined, again moving off. “Oh! I was going to warn ye against—but never mind, never mind—it’s all one, all in the family too;—sharp frost this morning, ain’t it? Good-bye to ye. Shan’t see ye again very soon, I guess; unless it’s before the Grand Jury.” And with these cracked words he finally departed, leaving me, for the moment, in no small wonderment at his frantic impudence.

At last, stepping on board the Pequod, we found everything in profound quiet, not a soul moving. The cabin entrance was locked within; the hatches were all on, and lumbered with coils of rigging. Going forward to the forecastle, we found the slide of the scuttle open. Seeing a light, we went down, and found only an old rigger there, wrapped in a tattered pea-jacket. He was thrown at whole length upon two chests, his face downwards and inclosed in his folded arms. The profoundest slumber slept upon him.

“Those sailors we saw, Queequeg, where can they have gone to?” said I, looking dubiously at the sleeper. But it seemed that, when on the wharf, Queequeg had not at all noticed what I now alluded to; hence I would have thought myself to have been optically deceived in that matter, were it not for Elijah’s otherwise inexplicable question. But I beat the thing down; and again marking the sleeper, jocularly hinted to Queequeg that perhaps we had best sit up with the body; telling him to establish himself accordingly. He put his hand upon the sleeper’s rear, as though feeling if it was soft enough; and then, without more ado, sat quietly down there.
“Gracious! Queequeg, don’t sit there,” said I.
“Oh! perry dood seat,” said Queequeg, “my country way; won’t hurt him face.”

“Face!” said I, “call that his face? very benevolent countenance then; but how hard he breathes, he’s heaving himself; get off, Queequeg, you are heavy, it’s grinding the face of the poor. Get off, Queequeg! Look, he’ll twitch you off soon. I wonder he don’t wake.”

Queequeg removed himself to just beyond the head of the sleeper, and lighted his tomahawk pipe. I sat at the feet. We kept the pipe passing over the sleeper, from one to the other. Meanwhile, upon questioning him in his broken fashion, Queequeg gave me to understand that, in his land, owing to the absence of settees and sofas of all sorts, the king, chiefs, and great people generally, were in the custom of fattening some of the lower orders for ottomans; and to furnish a house comfortably in that respect, you had only to buy up eight or ten lazy fellows, and lay them round in the piers and alcoves. Besides, it was very convenient on an excursion; much better than those garden-chairs which are convertible into walking-sticks; upon occasion, a chief calling his attendant, and desiring him to make a settee of himself under a spreading tree, perhaps in some damp marshy place.
While narrating these things, every time Queequeg received the tomahawk from me, he flourished the hatchet-side of it over the sleeper’s head.
“What’s that for, Queequeg?”
“Perry easy, kill-e; oh! perry easy!”

He was going on with some wild reminiscences about his tomahawk-pipe, which, it seemed, had in its two uses both brained his foes and soothed his soul, when we were directly attracted to the sleeping rigger. The strong vapor now completely filling the contracted hole, it began to tell upon him. He breathed with a sort of muffledness; then seemed troubled in the nose; then revolved over once or twice; then sat up and rubbed his eyes.
“Holloa!” he breathed at last, “who be ye smokers?”
“Shipped men,” answered I, “when does she sail?”
“Aye, aye, ye are going in her, be ye? She sails to-day. The Captain came aboard last night.”
“What Captain?—Ahab?”
“Who but him indeed?”
I was going to ask him some further questions concerning Ahab, when we heard a noise on deck.
“Holloa! Starbuck’s astir,” said the rigger. “He’s a lively chief mate, that; good man, and a pious; but all alive now, I must turn to.” And so saying he went on deck, and we followed.

It was now clear sunrise. Soon the crew came on board in twos and threes; the riggers bestirred themselves; the mates were actively engaged; and several of the shore people were busy in bringing various last things on board. Meanwhile Captain Ahab remained invisibly enshrined within his cabin.

modern_en.title: Chapter 21 — Going Aboard
paragraphs: It was nearly six o'clock, but only a gray, imperfect, misty dawn when we approached the wharf.
"There are some sailors running ahead there, if I'm seeing right," said I to Queequeg. "Those can't be shadows. She must be leaving by sunrise, I think. Come on!"

"Stop!" cried a voice. Its owner came up close behind us, laid a hand on both our shoulders, and then slipped himself in between us. Stooping forward slightly in the uncertain twilight, he peered strangely from Queequeg to me. It was Elijah.
"Going aboard?"
"Hands off, will you," said I.
"Look here," said Queequeg, shaking himself free, "go away!"
"Not going aboard, then?"
"Yes, we are," said I, "but what business is that of yours? Do you know, Mr. Elijah, that I consider you rather rude?"
"No, no, no — I wasn't aware of that," said Elijah, slowly and wonderingly looking from me to Queequeg and back with the strangest glances.
"Elijah," said I, "you would do my friend and me a favor by going away. We're heading to the Indian and Pacific Oceans and would prefer not to be delayed."
"Are you, are you? Coming back before breakfast?"
"He's crazy, Queequeg," said I. "Come on."
"Hello there!" cried Elijah, standing where he was and calling after us when we had gone a few steps.
"Ignore him," said I. "Queequeg, come on."
But he crept up to us again and, suddenly clapping his hand on my shoulder, said, "Did you see anything that looked like men heading toward that ship a little while ago?"
Struck by this straightforward, matter-of-fact question, I answered, "Yes, I thought I saw four or five men, but it was too dim to be sure."
"Very dim, very dim," said Elijah. "Morning to you."
Once more we left him behind. But once more he came softly after us, and touching my shoulder again, said, "See if you can find them now, will you?"
"Find who?"

"Morning to you! Morning to you!" he called back, moving off again. "Oh! I was going to warn you against — but never mind, never mind — it's all one, all in the family too. Sharp frost this morning, isn't it? Goodbye to you. Won't be seeing you again very soon, I guess — unless it's before the Grand Jury." And with those wild words he finally departed, leaving me for the moment in no small amazement at his frantic boldness.

At last, stepping aboard the Pequod, we found everything in deep quiet. Not a soul was moving. The cabin entrance was locked from inside. The hatches were all closed and piled with coils of rigging. Going forward to the forecastle, we found the scuttle slide open. Seeing a light, we went down and found only an old rigger there, wrapped in a tattered pea jacket. He was stretched out full length across two sea chests, face down, his head buried in his folded arms. The deepest sleep had taken hold of him.

"Those sailors we saw, Queequeg — where could they have gone?" said I, looking doubtfully at the sleeper. But it seemed that Queequeg hadn't noticed what I was referring to when we were on the wharf. I would have thought I was seeing things, if not for Elijah's otherwise inexplicable question. But I pushed the thought aside. Looking again at the sleeper, I jokingly suggested to Queequeg that perhaps we should sit up with the body, and told him to make himself comfortable. He put his hand on the sleeper's rear end, as if testing whether it was soft enough, and then, without further hesitation, sat right down on it.
"Good gracious! Queequeg, don't sit there," said I.
"Oh! Very good seat," said Queequeg. "My country way. Won't hurt him face."

"Face!" said I. "You call that his face? A very benevolent face, then. But listen to how hard he's breathing — he's heaving up and down. Get off, Queequeg, you're heavy. It's grinding the face of the poor. Get off, Queequeg! Look, he'll throw you off any second. I'm amazed he doesn't wake up."

Queequeg moved himself just past the sleeper's head and lit his tomahawk pipe. I sat at the feet. We passed the pipe back and forth over the sleeper between us. Meanwhile, when I questioned him, Queequeg explained in his broken way that in his land, due to the complete lack of benches and sofas, the king, chiefs, and important people had the custom of fattening some of the lower orders to serve as ottomans; and to furnish a house comfortably in that respect, you only had to buy up eight or ten lazy fellows and lay them around in the wall spaces between the windows and in the alcoves. Besides, they were very convenient on outings — much better than those garden chairs that fold into walking sticks. On occasion, a chief would simply call his attendant and order him to make himself into a bench under a spreading tree, perhaps in some damp marshy spot.
While telling these stories, every time Queequeg took the tomahawk from me, he flourished the hatchet end of it over the sleeper's head.
"What's that for, Queequeg?"
"Very easy, kill him. Oh! Very easy!"

He was going on with some wild memories about his tomahawk-pipe, which had apparently both brained his enemies and soothed his soul, when we were suddenly drawn to the sleeping rigger. The thick smoke had completely filled the cramped space and was starting to affect him. He breathed with a sort of muffled sound, then seemed bothered in his nose, then rolled over once or twice, then sat up and rubbed his eyes.
"Hey there!" he finally wheezed. "Who are you smokers?"
"Signed-on crew," I answered. "When does she sail?"
"Oh, you're going on her, are you? She sails today. The captain came aboard last night."
"What captain — Ahab?"
"Who else?"
I was about to ask him more questions about Ahab when we heard noise on deck.

"Hey! Starbuck's up and about," said the rigger. "He's a sharp chief mate, that one — good man and religious. But he's fully awake now, so I've got to get to work." And with that he went up on deck, and we followed.

It was now clear sunrise. Soon the crew came aboard in twos and threes. The riggers got to work. The mates were busy giving orders. And several people from shore were bringing various last things on board. Meanwhile, Captain Ahab remained invisibly enshrined within his cabin.

modern_da.title: Kapitel 21 — Om bord
paragraphs: Klokken var næsten seks, men det var kun en grå, ufuldkommen, tåget daggry, da vi nærmede os kajen.
»Der er nogle sømænd, der løber foran, hvis jeg ser ret,« sagde jeg til Queequeg. »Det kan ikke være skygger. Hun skal vist afsted ved solopgang. Kom!«

»Stop!« råbte en stemme. Dens ejer kom helt tæt bag os, lagde en hånd på hver af vores skuldre og trængte sig så ind imellem os. Han bøjede sig lidt frem i det usikre tusmørke og kiggede sært fra Queequeg til mig. Det var Elijah.
»På vej om bord?«
»Fingrene væk, vil du ikke nok,« sagde jeg.
»Hør her,« sagde Queequeg og rystede sig fri, »gå væk!«
»Så skal I ikke om bord?«
»Jo, det skal vi,« sagde jeg, »men hvad kommer det dig ved? Ved du, Mr. Elijah, at jeg synes, du er ret uforskammet?«
»Nej, nej, nej — det var jeg ikke klar over,« sagde Elijah langsomt og forundret og så fra mig til Queequeg og tilbage med de sælsomste blikke.
»Elijah,« sagde jeg, »du ville gøre min ven og mig en tjeneste ved at gå din vej. Vi skal til Det Indiske Ocean og Stillehavet og vil helst ikke forsinkes.«
»Skal I, skal I? Kommer I tilbage før morgenmad?«
»Han er gal, Queequeg,« sagde jeg. »Kom nu.«
»Hallo dér!« råbte Elijah, der blev stående, hvor han var, og kaldte efter os, da vi var gået nogle skridt.
»Lad som ingenting,« sagde jeg. »Queequeg, kom nu.«
Men han krøb hen til os igen og sagde, mens han pludselig klappede hånden på min skulder: »Så I noget, der lignede mænd på vej mod det skib for lidt siden?«
Overrasket over dette ligefremme, jævne spørgsmål svarede jeg: »Ja, jeg syntes, jeg så fire eller fem mænd, men det var for utydeligt til at være sikker.«
»Meget utydeligt, meget utydeligt,« sagde Elijah. »Morgen til dig.«
Endnu en gang forlod vi ham. Men endnu en gang kom han lydløst efter os, rørte ved min skulder igen og sagde: »Se, om I kan finde dem nu, vil I ikke?«
»Finde hvem?«

»Godmorgen til dig! Godmorgen til dig!« råbte han tilbage og gik videre. »Åh! Jeg ville advare dig mod — men lad det ligge, lad det ligge — det er lige meget, det er også kun inden for familien. Skarp frost i morges, ikke? Farvel med dig. Vi ses nok ikke så snart igen, tror jeg — medmindre det er foran nævningetinget.« Og med de vilde ord forsvandt han endelig og efterlod mig for en stund helt målløs over hans vanvittige frækhed.

Da vi endelig var kommet om bord på Pequod, lå alting i dyb ro. Ikke en sjæl rørte sig. Indgangen til kahytten var låst indefra. Lugerne var alle lukket og dækket med tove. Vi gik frem til mandskabsrummet og fandt lugen åben. Vi så et lys, gik ned og fandt kun en gammel rigger der, svøbt i en laset pjæk. Han lå udstrakt på tværs af to sømandskister med ansigtet nedad og hovedet begravet i sine foldede arme. Den dybeste søvn havde grebet ham.

»De sømænd, vi så, Queequeg — hvor kan de være blevet af?« sagde jeg og så tvivlende på den sovende. Men Queequeg havde åbenbart ikke lagt mærke til, hvad jeg mente, dengang vi stod på kajen. Jeg ville have troet, at jeg havde set syner, hvis ikke Elijahs ellers uforklarlige spørgsmål havde været. Men jeg skubbede tanken fra mig. Jeg så igen på den sovende og foreslog i spøg Queequeg, at vi måske skulle sidde ved liget, og bad ham gøre sig det behageligt. Han lagde hånden på den sovendes bagdel, som om han ville prøve, om den var blød nok, og satte sig så uden videre betænkning lige oven på den.
»Du godeste! Queequeg, sid ikke dér,« sagde jeg.
»Åh! Meget godt sæde,« sagde Queequeg. »Min land måde. Gør ikke ondt ansigt hans.«

»Ansigt!« sagde jeg. »Kalder du det hans ansigt? Så er det et meget venligt ansigt. Men hør, hvor tungt han trækker vejret — han hæver og sænker sig. Rejs dig, Queequeg, du er tung. Du trykker ansigtet ned på de fattige. Rejs dig, Queequeg! Se, han kaster dig af når som helst. Jeg undrer mig over, at han ikke vågner.«

Queequeg flyttede sig lige forbi den sovendes hoved og tændte sin tomahawk-pibe. Jeg satte mig ved fødderne. Vi rakte piben frem og tilbage hen over den sovende mellem os. Imens forklarede Queequeg på sit gebrokne sprog, da jeg spurgte ham, at kongen, høvdingene og de fornemme folk i hans land, fordi der slet ikke fandtes bænke og sofaer, havde for skik at fede nogle af de lavere stænder op, så de kunne tjene som ottomaner. For at indrette et hus bekvemt i den henseende behøvede man kun at købe otte eller ti dovne fyre op og lægge dem rundt i murfladerne mellem vinduerne og i alkoverne. Desuden var de meget praktiske på udflugter — meget bedre end de havestole, der kan klappes sammen til vandrestokke. Nogle gange kaldte en høvding bare på sin tjener og befalede ham at gøre sig til en bænk under et bredkronet træ, måske et fugtigt, sumpet sted.
Mens han fortalte de historier, svingede Queequeg, hver gang han tog tomahawken fra mig, økseenden hen over den sovendes hoved.
»Hvad er det til, Queequeg?«
»Meget let, dræbe ham. Åh! Meget let!«

Han var i gang med nogle vilde minder om sin tomahawk-pibe, som åbenbart både havde slået hjernen ud på hans fjender og beroliget hans sjæl, da vi pludselig blev revet ud af det af den sovende rigger. Den tykke røg havde fyldt det snævre rum helt op og begyndte at gå ham på. Han trak vejret med en slags dæmpet lyd, så virkede han generet i næsen, så rullede han rundt en-to gange, så satte han sig op og gned sig i øjnene.
»Hej dér!« hvæsede han endelig. »Hvem er I, I rygere?«
»Hyret mandskab,« svarede jeg. »Hvornår sejler hun?«
»Nå, skal I med hende? Hun sejler i dag. Kaptajnen kom om bord i nat.«
»Hvilken kaptajn — Ahab?«
»Hvem ellers?«
Jeg ville lige til at spørge ham mere om Ahab, da vi hørte larm på dækket.

»Hold da op! Starbuck er oppe,« sagde riggeren. »Han er en skarp første styrmand, den dér — en god mand og gudfrygtig. Men nu er han helt vågen, så jeg må i gang med arbejdet.« Og så gik han op på dækket, og vi fulgte efter.

Det var nu klar solopgang. Snart kom mandskabet om bord, to og tre ad gangen. Riggerne gik i gang. Styrmændene havde travlt med at give ordrer. Og flere folk fra land bragte forskellige sidste ting om bord. Imens forblev kaptajn Ahab usynlig, indesluttet som en helgen i sin kahyt.
